Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does two things, and they deserve different verdicts. Sections 1–5 are a careful, valuable re-analysis. Sections 6–8 and the conclusion claim much more than the evidence supports, and they ignore evidence the authors themselves cite.

## What holds up

- **The arithmetic checks out.** Table 2 is right (95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%). So are the hours falls (−14.1%, −13.9%) and the real revenue figure (1.014/1.041 ≈ −2.6%).
- **The attrition finding is the most important contribution.** Seven of the nine withdrawals came *after* the schedule began, and most cited inability to maintain output. That directly contradicts the working paper's "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." It is a factual misstatement the Halden authors should correct, not just a matter of interpretation.
- **The manager-versus-records comparison is well designed.** 19 of 23 organisations sit in the same direction, and the authors are measured in not alleging bad faith. The subset's manager index (98.9) is close to the full sample's (98.7), which suggests the 23 aren't unusually optimistic.
- **The data note honestly acknowledges** that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## Major problems

**1. The conclusion contradicts the randomised evidence the comment relies on.**
- The comment calls the Varden counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature." The same trial's case-processing stratum avoids every problem the comment lists:
  - It was randomised, so there is no selection.
  - Output came from records and hours from timesheets, so there is no measurement artifact.
  - It ran for nine months, longer than Halden.
  - It found output per FTE essentially unchanged and **+12.5% output per actual hour** (CI +6.9 to +18.4).
- The comment never mentions this result. Citing one stratum of a trial as definitive while ignoring the other is selective.
- The comment's own corrected estimate (+10.8%) is close to Varden's +12.5%. Two studies with different designs converging on a gain of roughly 10–12% per hour in non-coverage work points to a real effect, not an artifact.
- "Entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" is also stated about "reduced-hours schemes" in general, a claim that goes well beyond a re-analysis of one pilot.

**2. Attrition is listed as corrected, but it isn't.**
- The abstract says the 10.8% comes from "correcting the first three" problems. Table 2 corrects only two: output measure and hours.
- Attrition is documented but never quantified. The comment shows the bias exists but not how large it is.
- The withdrawing organisations ran the schedule for one to two months, so partial outcome data may exist. Analysing all 70 enrolled organisations using that data, or bounding the effect under stated assumptions about the withdrawers, would turn this into a correction. That is exactly what the comment's own recommendation asks future studies to do.

**3. The novelty argument is untested, and the microdata could test it.**
- The case rests on two survey points: energy at +0.61 SD at month 3 and +0.29 SD at month 6. That is self-reported energy, not output.
- **Extrapolation.** Fitting a straight line through two points is unjustified, since a plateau is equally consistent with the data. The extrapolation is also off: that line reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten."
- **The direct test was available and wasn't run.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*. Whether record-based output per hour fell between months 3 and 6 is the obvious test of novelty, and the comment uses the same microdata without running it.
- **The burden-of-proof claim cuts both ways.** "Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one" is true. But it means the comment can't conclude novelty either. The abstract says "plausibly a novelty effect"; the conclusion treats it as established.

**4. The critique of the meetings analysis misdescribes it.**
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** The Varden meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, three months before the nine-month results. The seven offices are simply the pre-registered treated case-processing stratum, not a subgroup chosen post hoc.
- **"Suggest this as a mechanism."** The Varden authors explicitly wrote that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," labelled the analysis unregistered, and registered a confirmatory test. The fair criticism is narrower: their Summary mentions the finding without flagging it as unregistered.
- **Supporting evidence goes unmentioned.** In Halden's own interviews, 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings.
- **The standards are asymmetric.** The comment dismisses a mechanism backed by a correlation across 7 offices plus interviews, while asserting a novelty mechanism backed by two survey points.

## Problems in the re-analysis itself

**5. Table 2 changes the sample between rows.**
- The four rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The step from +23.4% to +10.8% therefore mixes the effect of each correction with changes in which organisations are included.
- All specifications should be shown on the 17-organisation subset: manager index with scheduled hours, then with each correction separately, then both. That would give a clean decomposition.
- The sector composition of each subset should be reported. The 17 should also be reweighted to the full sample's sector mix, because coverage-bound organisations would shift the results.
- The comment should say whether its means are employee-weighted like Halden's. If not, the comparison with 23.4% isn't like for like.

**6. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.**
- Longer days of +0.7 hours across four days, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, adds 4.4 hours to a 32-hour schedule, giving about 36.4 hours. Starting from baseline-length days gives about 36.6.
- The reported figure is 34.6. Either the per-day figure is wrong or the components are defined differently, and the authors should reconcile them.

**7. Some record-based measures are themselves hours.**
- "Billable hours delivered" falls mechanically when hours are cut. Using it as output partly measures time, which biases output per hour toward zero in the subset.
- The authors should state how many of the 23 organisations used it and show results without them.

## Smaller points

- **Revenue.** CPI isn't the ideal deflator for business revenue; sector output-price deflators are better. The basic point stands. Revenue also doesn't feed into the per-hour figure, so the abstract shouldn't count it among the problems that "account for" the gain.
- **Retail sample size.** The retail figure from records (−11.2%) rests on three organisations and should be flagged as such. Its closeness to Varden's −11.4% is suggestive, but they measure different things: output per organisation versus output per FTE in public counters.
- **Unaccounted withdrawal.** Six withdrawals cited workload and two cited scheduling, leaving one reason unreported.

## Overall

A defensible conclusion from this evidence would be:

> Halden overstated the per-hour gain by more than half. Correcting the output measure and the hours denominator leaves about 11% in a non-random subset, and attrition bias, still unquantified, would lower it further. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours cut output. Whether the residual gain lasts is unresolved. It is consistent with the randomised Varden case-processing estimate.

That would still be a strong comment. The current conclusion, "entirely an artifact," doesn't follow from the comment's own data.

Across the three documents, the evidence now looks fairly consistent:
- **Non-coverage work:** output per employee roughly unchanged, actual hours down about 13–14%, output per actual hour up about 10–12%.
- **Coverage-bound work:** output down about 11%.
- **Durability:** still unknown.

I can write this up as a referee report on the comment, or as a short synthesis of all three papers.
